question: Does the Qur'an misunderstand the Trinity by saying Christians take three gods, including Mary?
asked: I have a colleague at work who is a believing Christian, and we have a lot of discussions about Islam and the Qur'an. He says the Qur'an does not understand the Trinity and that, a'udhu billah, the Prophet ﷺ made a mistake: the Qur'an says Christians believe in three gods and that Jesus and Mary are part of the Trinity. He says this is completely false: no Christian has ever said there are three gods, and Jesus and Mary have never been considered part of the Trinity. How do we understand these verses in the Qur'an?
answer:
Now, the primary verses that deal with Christian theology, there are three. So pay heed to these, and inshallah we'll dissect them and explain them in a holistic manner.

First is Surah An-Nisa verse 171, where Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala says, "Believe in Allah and His messengers, and do not say three," wa la taqulu thalathah. Notice, the word used here for three is thalathah, which is three: one, two, three. It's not the Arabic word for Trinity, which is tathlith, or other words that are used. So the point being that this word three is being understood to mean three actual entities. And then Allah says, intahu khayran lakum, "Stop saying three, it is better for you." Surah Nisa verse 171.

The second is Surah Al-Ma'idah verse 73. Allah says: those who say that Allah is the third of a three have committed kufr. Those who say that Allah is the third of a three, thalithu thalathah. So there are three entities, and Allah is one of them, the third of them. The third here doesn't necessarily mean in chronological order; it simply means one of the three is Allah. Once again, what is being affirmed are three entities, and that Allah is one of those three. So Allah is saying that anybody who says that Allah is three, or a part of a three, or one third of a three, anybody who says this has committed kufr. Wa ma min ilahin illa ilahun wahid: there's only one God.

And lastly, Surah Al-Ma'idah verse 116, where Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala says, "Ya 'Isa ibn Maryam": 'Isa will be asked on the Day of Judgment by Allah, "O Jesus, did you tell people to take you and your mother as gods instead of Allah?" So here Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala is asking 'Isa ibn Maryam: did you tell people to take you and your mother as gods, ilahayn, two gods besides Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala? And 'Isa will say, "Glory be to You, I could never say anything other than what You commanded me to say," and the verses go on.

Now, these are not the only three, but these are the primary three verses in the Qur'an that deal with Christian theology.

Now, of course, mainstream Christian doctrine, which has been fairly consistent since the Nicene Creed of the third, fourth century, is that there is one God, but that one God exists in three co-eternal, consubstantial persons. And the technical term is hypostases: these three are distinct, and yet they are one in substance and one in nature. So the three hypostases are one. And so the doctrine of Christianity is that there are no three gods; rather, there are three distinct, yet one in substance and one in nature.

Now, obviously there's a lot of internal discussion on what this means. But the point that this Christian colleague is telling his Muslim colleague is that no Christian sect has ever said that there are three gods, and no Christian sect ever made Mary a part of the Trinity.

And this is, of course, a very common theory by polemicists, by those that are criticizing Islam, by Christians who try to find fault with Islam. What they end up doing is that they always say, "Oh, the author of the Qur'an" (and by this they obviously mean the Prophet ﷺ), "the author of the Qur'an didn't know Christian theology," they say, "and so the Qur'anic language is incorrect, because nobody actually says this."

Now, a number of points to be said here. And obviously this is a very convoluted topic. We can spend many, many hours talking about Christian theology, talking about these verses of the Qur'an and how they've been understood by over 50, 60 mufassirun throughout the eras. Obviously this is a short answer to a much longer topic.

However, **the claim that the Qur'an is unaware that Christians believe in monotheism is simply false.** The Qur'an is very clear. Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala says in Surah Al-'Ankabut, verse 46, "Do not argue with the People of the Book except in the manner that is best." And then the verses go on, and then Allah says, "And say to them": your ilah and our ilah is one and the same. You believe in one God, we believe in one God, and it is the same God, and we have submitted unto Him. So the Qur'an is very clear that Christians believe in one God. This is explicit in the Qur'an.

So then how do we understand these other verses that seem to imply that Christians believe in three gods? And the term for this is tritheism. Tritheism is the belief in three gods.

Now, it is true to say that some of our mufassirun did seem to understand this from the Qur'an. If you look, for example, at Muqatil ibn Sulayman and others, the understanding that they get from these verses is that Christians believe in three separate and distinct gods. And of course, as we said, this is not and has never been the belief of mainstream Christianity.

If you look at the majority of mufassirun, the scholars of tafsir, they really kind of gloss over this point. They don't really dive into deep Christology or the beliefs of Christians. And of course, we excuse them for this, because obviously even most Christians are unaware of the development of Christian doctrine and the wordings of the Nicene Creed. The Nicene Creed uses the term homoousios. I'm sure I'm mispronouncing the Greek term here; I have not studied Greek professionally. But homoousios is the term in the Nicene Creed, and what it means is that God the Father and God the Son and God the Holy Spirit have the same essence. Homo is "the same," ousios is "the essence" here. So they are unique in essence, despite the fact that they are three.

Now, as I said, the majority of mufassirun don't really dissect these verses. They just give a generic tafsir and then they move on. However, some of them, clearly the ones that are more well-read in Christianity than others, do point out that some more unpacking needs to be done. Of them, for example, is Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, definitely one of the more well-read of our scholars. He read many other traditions and many other books as well, many other philosophies. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi actually notes, when he talks about these verses, that no Christian group ever claimed that Jesus and Mary were gods besides Allah. He actually writes this in his tafsir, and he says, "How do we answer this?" And he proposes his answer. Other scholars attempted other explanations.

Again, the scholars that actually dive deep into this are those that are more well-read in Christianity. And again, I've said this a million times: all of our scholars are humans. All of our scholars have their, masha'Allah, strengths, but they're not all knowledgeable, especially in Christian theology. One would expect that the majority of our mufassirun never really studied in depth what Christians say. Those that did study were those that interacted with other civilizations, and especially those that lived in Andalus.

And that is why, for example, Ibn Hazm has a position. Ibn Hazm said that this must be one of the non-existent Christian groups. And he actually mentions one; he calls it the Barbaraniyyah, the Barbaraniyyah group. And he said that this was a group that believed that Jesus and his mother were two gods besides Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. They actually believed this, according to him. And he says this sect is now extinct. So the Qur'an, he is saying, is referencing sects and schisms that no longer exist. And this notion was taken up by a number of authors, including Suyuti and his teacher in their Tafsir al-Jalalayn. They also mentioned this point as well.

The problem with this is that, firstly, we are not sure if there was any such sect. There's really no confirmed evidence that such a sect existed. And secondly, even if it did for sure, it was a very fringe, very small sect. It wasn't mainstream even at the time of the Prophet ﷺ. Why would the Qur'an reference something that was never common amongst Christians? And also the main point: we are not even certain whether there ever was such a sect.

Imam al-Qurtubi as well. And again, Qurtubi is from Cordova; Qurtubi was interacting with Christians. Again, we expect him to be more knowledgeable of Christianity than many of the other scholars of tafsir. And Imam al-Qurtubi also problematizes this notion of Christian theology vis-a-vis these verses: how does one reconcile Christian theology with these verses? And Imam al-Qurtubi says, this is not what Christians believe. So he says, look, what the verse is saying outwardly is not the technical belief of the Christians. But then he says, it is the lazim madhhabihim: it is the corollary, what the beliefs that the Christians hold necessitate.

So Imam al-Qurtubi points out that even if the terms that the Qur'an is using are not the technical terminology, it is what Christian theology necessitates. That's what is called the lazim al-madhhab, or the corollaries: basically, when you say something, what do you necessarily imply by it? So the Qur'anic terminology is not what the Christians say; it is the logical follow-up. It is the inevitable conclusion of what they say.

Now, obviously, as I explained, from the polemical Christian side, from the Orientalists, and then those that are trying to criticize Islam, they claim that essentially the Qur'an is misinformed, or the author of the Qur'an is misinformed or uninformed about the Trinity. And this was a common motif. Even Montgomery Watt, probably the most famous Orientalist of the last generation, also claimed this: that it is very clear that, quote unquote, the author of the Qur'an was unaware of Christian theology.

Now, how then do we explain all of this? I have two explanations, and both of them are valid. There's no either/or here; both of them are valid.

The first thing that we need to do is to actually look up: what did Arab Christians believe when the Qur'an came down? Because, you see, most Western historians, when they talk about Christianity, are talking about the Christianity of Rome or the Christianity of Constantinople, and they're not really looking at the Christianity of the Arabs. And among the Arabs at the time of Islam, when the Qur'an came down, there were two primary Arab Christians: you had the Christians of Najran, and then you had the Ghassanids. These were the two primary Christians.

As for the Ghassanids, there were a number of altercations between them and the Prophet ﷺ and the Sahabah; even the Battle of Tabuk was basically supposed to be against them. As for the Christians of Najran, they're the ones that came to visit the Prophet ﷺ, and they stayed in Medina and they interacted with him, and Allah revealed Qur'an regarding them. So these are the two primary Christians that Islam, or the early Muslims, interacted with, and the Qur'an is being revealed in that milieu, in that context.

So what we need to do is actually understand the theology of Arab Christians, the Christian Arabs of the fifth and early sixth century. And the problem is that we hardly have any remnants of their teachings, of their beliefs, because the Arab civilization by and large did not leave us records. They didn't have books written at that time. It was a very different time and world and place, and it is difficult to reconstruct the detailed theology of the Arab Christians.

Nonetheless, in the research that I've done, I looked up a number of things in this regard. First and foremost, there is a massive, very, very erudite encyclopedia, or encyclopedic reference, by Professor Irfan Shahid, who is actually an Arab Christian himself. Well, he's passed away, but of the last generation. And he taught at Georgetown for, I think, more than two, three decades. And he wrote, I think, a seven-, eight-volume encyclopedia about Arab Christianity. And of course, he himself was a Christian Arab, so obviously he has a personal interest as well.

And if you look up this book, in volume six he mentions some research that he's done. Again, it's sketchy. He did this three decades ago, I think in the 60s, 70s; I'm not sure exactly when. But he mentions in this book that the Ghassanids were influenced by the famous Christian theologian John Philoponus, who died 570, i.e. at the time the Prophet ﷺ is born.

Basically, there was a very, very famous Christian theologian, John Philoponus. He's well known to Christian scholars, and he is also well known to scholars of Arabic intellectual history, because his works were translated into Arabic, and he's called Yahya al-Nahwi, John the Grammarian. And John Philoponus, very interestingly, had an impact on the Ghassanid Arabs, and he was considered to be a heretic by the mainstream Christianity of Constantinople. And part of his heresy was that he was accused by his contemporaries of tritheism. This is very interesting. He was accused, even though he didn't say those wordings, but his beliefs were almost bordering on three distinct gods. And so in his own lifetime and after his death, he was accused of basically propagating tritheism.

And we know, according to research done, that the Ghassanid Arabs had been influenced by John Philoponus and that they had absorbed this theology. If that is the case, which does appear to be the case, then in reality the Qur'anic language is very, very precise. And it is amazing that the Qur'an is using terminology that would not be mainstream in Constantinople per se, but it would be mainstream amongst the audience that is listening to the Qur'an.

Now, this idea has been further researched a few years ago by another academic, Professor Block, in an article that he wrote for the Journal of Islamic Studies entitled "Philoponian Monophysitism in South Arabia at the Advent of Islam with Implications for the English Translation of Thalatha in the Qur'an." This is an entire academic article.

And by the way, subhanAllah, there's so much research being done by people outside of our faith. Now, a lot of that research is obviously sometimes very problematic, and sometimes it's not. And the point is that there must be some people who are willing to go beyond, because this is knowledge that, really, frankly, our own did not and cannot have, because it deals with civilizations and languages that are not found. I mean, we cannot expect somebody to know Philoponian monophysitism that's going on in Christian communities and other places in the world. So you have people that are outside of our faith tradition doing some really interesting research, and those that read that research then take the good from it. Because again, wisdom and knowledge transcends any one civilization, history, research. You don't have to be a Muslim to do research in science and engineering and history. The knowledge is there. And those that are willing and are capable, they should venture out and get the best of all worlds. And when they do that, obviously they will be slightly different than... anyway, that's beside the point here.

But my point is that some research has been done. And if you read this journal article, he actually argues about the Christian Arabs of Najran. So he talked about the Ghassanids; now he is saying the Christian Arabs of Najran. Another professor, Professor Block, has done research about Southern Arabian Christianity, and he has concluded that it is very likely that the Christian Arabs of Najran were de facto tritheistic, i.e. their beliefs and their understanding was that there are three distinct gods, again being influenced by Philoponian, i.e. John Philoponus, Philoponian monophysitism. So this is again the technical term for his beliefs here.

Now, this is particularly interesting, because realize, Surah Nisa and Surah Al-Ma'idah were revealed because of the Christians of Najran. They were revealed after the Christians of Najran visited Medina, and the Qur'an is then addressing them. And it is really impossible for us to imagine that an average person in Arabia would know the differences between Southern Arabian Christianity versus the Christianity of Rome versus the Christianity of Constantinople. Only Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala could have been so precise that He is speaking to them in a language that they will understand. And He's refuting them directly, and then He's refuting other Christians indirectly.

And therefore we will flip it around. This colleague of our brother's is saying that the author is misinformed. We say, rather, you are misinformed, and the Qur'an is being infinitely more precise than would have been possible. The Qur'an is challenging the beliefs that were in vogue amongst Arab Christians, using the terminology and a language that is rebuking them for what they believe. And the fact that Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala distinguished between their versions of Christianity versus others could not come from an average person living in Arabia.

Now, that is my first response. We can add to this response, and it is a very good answer as well. I also like and agree with this one, and there's no contradiction; we can give both of these responses. This is a response that has been proposed by a number of researchers, and I myself am very much inclined towards it. And of the researchers that propose this is a friend of mine from Yale, Joseph Cummings. We were together in the department, and he has a PhD about certain issues of this nature, and we had a lot of discussion about this while I was there. And he also has this type of notion.

And in summary, what it argues is that **the Qur'an is using the language of popular belief and not the language of abstract creeds.** So in other words, the Qur'an is dealing with the lived experience of Christians, and the Qur'an is calling them out. Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala is rebuking them for essentially deifying Mary and Jesus, even if they don't use the word God for Mary. Because, again, the Qur'an says that you have taken Mary and Jesus as gods. And the Christian says, "We never say Mary is a God." And the response is: we don't care what you say.

Now, remember, we're talking about the Christianity pre-Reformation. My audience here in America is more aware of Protestant Christianity. Martin Luther, it is very clear that he was influenced by many factors, including the Qur'an. Martin Luther read the Qur'an. Martin Luther's version of Christianity clearly is closer to our version of tawhid than Catholic Christianity. And you have to realize, before Martin Luther, obviously, the default in the world was the Catholic version of Christianity. And in Catholic Christianity, Mary is invoked for one's needs. People invoke the Virgin Mary. And if you go to a Catholic church, you will find icons of Mary and Jesus. And if you go to a Protestant church, you're not going to find that, because again of the whole notion of the iconoclastic battle between the two groups, which, again, is not our answer here.

But my point is that Protestant Christianity, which is what most of my viewers are familiar with, is very different than the Christianity before. Christianity before Protestantism, the mainstream Catholic and Orthodox and whatnot, their version of Christianity really did take Jesus and Mary as objects of worship (well, even Protestants do Jesus, but not Mary). And Allah is speaking to Christians with regards to their lived reality, and not with regards to the creeds that the advanced councils propagate.

In other words, they might say that God is one, but in reality, in their minds, God is three. They might say that Mary is not God, but when they invoke her and they praise her and they ask her for their needs, they have made her into a God, in that they believe she will respond to them directly. And so in their worship and in their psychological framework, Mary is a God, even if they don't use the term God.

And so Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala is using terminology that is very precise, not according to the sophisticated, developed statements by the councils in Rome or the councils in Nicaea or the councils in Constantinople or the councils in other places. They had like 12 different councils, one by one, and each one is named after the place and the locality, and each of these councils propagated Christian theology. SubhanAllah, Allah 'azza wa jall is basically saying: I don't care about your councils. Your councils mean nothing. What is the lived religion? How do Christians actually live? What do they view the Trinity as? How do they deal with Jesus and with Mary? And so the Qur'anic terminology is in fact very precise, because Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala is dealing with the reality as it exists, and not how it is propagated in fancy councils.

And therefore we say that the Qur'an is referencing the belief of the common Christians, and especially the belief of the Arab Christians, and asking them to correct their misunderstandings in accordance with their actual shubuhat, their actual arguments.

And as for your friend who's criticizing Islam: your friend is lost in abstract creeds. So we say to him that rather than trying to find fault with the Qur'an, he should realize that the Qur'an is doing a much better and a much more precise job of challenging Christian belief and refuting it. And we say to this friend of yours (and please show him this video clip) that if he is a true Christian, he should ponder over what the Qur'an is saying, and in fact even what the Bible has said and what Jesus himself has said: that neither is there a Trinity, nor did Jesus ever preach a Trinity, nor did Jesus ever preach his own divinity, nor did Jesus ever say to worship him or to worship Mary. And this is exactly what the Qur'an says, and this is exactly what the New Testament and Jesus himself said.

So that is the response to our first question, and Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala knows best.
